Love or Control

What this study answers. (1) What is it called when people control or use others "in the name of love"? (2) What do people do or expect in love's name that is really something else, and what lies behind it (I-am-nots, unmet needs, fear, shame)? (3) Why do ordinary, loving people turn controlling or selfish? (4) When a parent or spouse says "I care, that's why I'm forcing this," what are the boundaries? (5) In the relational gospel, do we simply stand by while someone we love harms themselves? The answer in short: neither force nor abandonment; costly, truthful, non-coercive presence, plus real protection where someone cannot protect themselves.

Please read first. This is a study, not counselling, legal or medical advice. Everyone does some of this at times; the aim is to see it clearly and gently, in ourselves first. Words like "monster" describe how it can feel to the person on the receiving end; they are not a verdict on a person. If you are in an abusive or frightening situation, jump to Part 8 and the safety box.

PART 1 — What It Is Called: The Vocabulary

There is no single word. Different fields name different slices of the same pattern. Most of these are descriptive labels, not diagnoses, and a person can do some of them without malice or awareness.

TermWhat it meansExample in love's name
Emotional blackmail (Susan Forward)Using fear, obligation and guilt ("FOG") to make someone comply by threatening to withdraw love, approval or support"If you marry him, you're dead to me." "After everything I've done for you…"
Psychological control (Brian Barber)Parenting that intrudes on a child's thoughts, feelings and sense of self: guilt induction, shaming, love withdrawal, invalidating feelingsSilent treatment until the child gives in; "you're hurting your mother"
Conditional regard (Assor, Roth & Deci)Showing warmth and approval only when the child meets the parent's expectationsAffection when marks are high, coldness when they drop
Coercive control (Evan Stark)A pattern of domination in an intimate relationship: monitoring, isolating, controlling money, rules, threats. Often with warmth in between"I'm jealous because I love you"; checking the phone; choosing your friends and clothes
Enmeshment (Salvador Minuchin)Blurred boundaries: family members' feelings, decisions and identities are fused; separate opinions feel like betrayal"We are one family; your decision is everyone's business"
PaternalismOverriding a person's choices for their own good, treating a capable adult as a childHiding information; deciding a grown child's career
Love-bombing / intermittent affectionIntense affection and gifts, alternating with withdrawal, which makes the person work for approvalShowering warmth after a fight to restore compliance
Rescuer role (Karpman's drama triangle)Needing someone to stay helpless so that one can stay needed; "helping" that keeps the other dependentPaying off a grown child's every mistake and removing every consequence
Codependency (popular term)Finding one's worth and calm in managing another person's behaviour or problemsHovering, monitoring, covering up, or "I can't be okay unless you are"
Spiritual abuse / authoritarian spiritual controlUsing God, "covering", submission or fear of judgement to control decisions"God told me you shouldn't go there." "Questioning me is rebellion."

In the relational gospel's words: this is self-protection dressed as love. It uses another person to ease my own fear, shame or emptiness (the I-am-nots and unmet needs in earlier parts of this series), then names that "love." Biblical love, by contrast, "does not insist on its own way" (1 Cor 13:5).

PART 2 — Care vs Control: How to Tell

2.1 Two Ways to Fail, One Way to Love

Parenting research (Diana Baumrind's classic styles) and the Bible both warn of two errors, not one. Eli's sons ran wild because he "did not restrain them" (1 Sam 3:13); fathers are also told not to "provoke your children to anger" (Eph 6:4) lest they "lose heart" (Col 3:21). Love sits between neglect and control: warm, clear, explaining, and respecting the other's growing freedom.

2.2 Ten Differences Between Care and Control

QuestionCare saysControl says
Whose anxiety is being managed?The other's welfare is the main concernMine: "I can't sleep unless you obey"
Is "no" allowed?You may disagree and I stay warmA "no" brings anger, tears, silence or punishment
What happens to love when they choose differently?It staysIt is withdrawn or turns cold
Are reasons given and heard?Yes, and I may change my mind"Because I said so" or "you'll understand someday"
Does it fit the person's age and capacity?Restrictions shrink as maturity growsA 35-year-old is handled like a 10-year-old
Is it about one danger or about everything?Specific, serious riskPreferences, image and comfort presented as danger
Are tactics honest?Open request or concernGuilt, fear, hidden information, threats, comparison
Does the other become more or less themselves?More confident, honest and freeSmaller, secretive, anxious or rebellious
What is the track record?Trust grows over timeSecrecy and distance grow
Who benefits if they comply?Mainly themMainly me (calm, image, status, being needed)

2.3 What Research Suggests

  • Barber (1996, Child Development) distinguished psychological control (guilt, love withdrawal, invalidation) from behavioural control (rules, monitoring, supervision). Research in that tradition has linked psychological control to more anxiety, depression and problems with identity, while age-appropriate rules and supervision are not harmful in the same way. The difference is how the limit is held, not whether there is one.
  • Assor, Roth & Deci (2004, Journal of Personality) studied conditional regard and reported that it can produce compliance, but also internal pressure, resentment and unstable self-worth, even when the behaviour looks successful.
  • Self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan) argues that people flourish when they feel autonomy, competence and relatedness; control undermines autonomy and, over time, the quality of motivation.

These findings come mostly from Western samples, and cultures differ in how closeness, obedience and family decision-making are understood. Research on Asian families suggests the meaning of parental control varies, and warmth matters in every culture. These are correlations and summaries, not predictions for any one family.

PART 3 — What Is Underneath: I-Am-Nots and Needs

Control rarely begins as a plan to hurt. It usually begins as a fear that a person cannot bear. Underneath that fear is often an I-am-not ("I am not safe," "I am not enough," "I am not needed") or an unmet need (security, significance, belonging, being valued). The controlling sentence is the visible part; the iceberg below is where the real story lives.

3.1 Translating the Sentences: What Is Said vs What May Be Underneath

Said "in love"What may be underneathI-am-not / needWhat the other experiences
"Don't go; I love you."Fear of being left; the other's leaving feels like abandonmentI am abandoned; need for securityGuilt for having a life
"I'm only worried about you."Anxiety that cannot tolerate uncertainty; control relieves itI am not safe; need for safetyNot trusted; has to manage the worrier's feelings
"After all I've sacrificed…"Love turned into a debt; unvoiced hunger for recognitionI am not valued; need to be seenA gift becomes an invoice; love feels bought
"What will people say?"Honour and shame; the child as a reflection of the familyI am not acceptable; need for belongingValued as an image, not as a person
"I know what's best for you."Need to be the wise, needed one; own unlived life or own wounds projectedI am not significant; need for purposeTheir own mind is not trusted or wanted
"If you loved me, you would…"Love is measured by compliance; demands for proofI am not lovable; need for reassuranceLove is a test they can never pass
"I'm jealous because I love you."Insecurity; the partner's friends and freedom feel like threatsI am not enough; need for exclusivityShrinking world, monitoring, isolation
Silence, cold shoulder, sulkingWithdrawal of warmth as punishment; wound expressed through pressureI am not heard; need for significanceLearns love is earned by giving in
Constant rescuing, paying, fixingBeing needed is the source of worth; consequences feel unbearableI am not needed; need for purposeStays dependent, or feels owned
"God told me you shouldn't."Spiritual language used to make a personal fear unquestionableI am not in control; need for certaintyDisagreement feels like disobeying God

Caution. These are possible readings, not diagnoses. Sometimes the worry is simply accurate (the road really is dangerous). The test is the pattern: how the person responds to "no," to uncertainty, and to their own fear (Part 2.2).

3.2 Needs That Get Met Through Other People

A healthy need (security, significance, belonging) is meant to be received and then shared. When a need is unmet, a person may try to get it met from the other person, who then becomes the supplier. Compare:

NeedHealthy expressionControlling "love"
Security"I feel anxious when you travel; please text when you arrive." (a request)"You will not travel." (a demand that treats the other as the cure)
SignificanceGiving advice when asked, and being glad when it is used or notNeeding the other to follow the advice to feel respected
BelongingWanting closeness while allowing the other friends and a separate lifeTreating other relationships as threats or betrayals
Being valuedSaying "I'd love to hear that you appreciate it"Keeping a ledger of sacrifices to collect obedience

Relational gospel reading: the controller is looking for something real (safety, significance, belonging) in the wrong place. The Father is meant to be the source, so that I can love without needing you to be my security. "There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear, for fear has to do with punishment (kolasis)" (1 John 4:18). Control is how fear tries to run the relationship.
